intro: Munich protects its remarkable trees by law and number: a 2021 city ordinance registers 117 Naturdenkmäler covering 200 trees, each legally protected the way a listed building would be. That bureaucratic precision sits oddly with their origins: planted by a royal count's landscape garden, grown wild in a monastery orchard, set in the ground by twelve thousand schoolchildren celebrating a war's end. Two of the trees below carry rival claims to being the city's single oldest tree, and neither is settled. Munich has not tried to force the point.
meta_description: Munich protects 200 trees by city ordinance. Meet a 600-year-old oak, a hollow linden painted by an artist, and eight rare hackberries on a ring road.
question_answer: Munich has no single agreed oldest tree: two different trees carry the claim from different sources. The Krüner Eiche, a pedunculate oak in Sendling-Westpark, is cited by a district citizen assembly as roughly 600 years old, which would date it to the 1420s. The Röth-Linde in Moosach, a winter linden, is separately described by local press as the city's oldest tree at 300 to 350 years. The two claims have never been reconciled against each other. Just outside the city, the Edigna Lime of Puch near Fürstenfeldbruck is older than either, with estimates running from 500 to 1,200 years.
question_meta: Munich has two rival claims to its oldest tree, a 600-year-old oak and a 300-plus-year-old linden. Both, and the city's other protected trees, explained.
question_context: Munich's own tally is the most precise starting point any city on this list has offered: a 2021 ordinance names 117 protected Naturdenkmäler covering 200 individual trees across the city, each with a case made for rarity, size, beauty or historical association. Age is a different matter. Ring counts require felling a tree, so every age here comes from growth models, historical association or simple local reputation, not a verified count. The Krüner Eiche's roughly 600-year figure comes from a 2017 Sendling-Westpark district citizen assembly document arguing for the oak's preservation; the Röth-Linde's 300 to 350 year figure, and its billing as Munich's oldest tree, comes from a dedicated local news feature and the tree's own German Wikipedia page. Both are treated here as the honest, sourced claims they are rather than resolved into one winner. The Krüner Eiche stands at Krüner Platz in Sendling-Westpark, an eight minute walk from Harras U-Bahn station.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Munich?
faq.a: Two trees claim the title from different sources: the roughly 600-year-old Krüner Eiche oak in Sendling-Westpark, and the 300 to 350-year-old Röth-Linde in Moosach, separately called the city's oldest tree by local press. Neither claim has been checked against the other.

faq.q: How does Munich protect its old and remarkable trees?
faq.a: By city ordinance. A 2021 update to the Naturdenkmalverordnung lists 117 individually protected natural monuments covering 200 trees across Munich, each legally protected for its age, rarity, size or historical association.

faq.q: Where is the best place to see protected trees in Munich?
faq.a: The Englischer Garten holds three trees on this list within a short walk of each other: the oldest known elms in the city, a beech over 300 years old, and a rare fern-leaved beech cultivar, all in the park's southern half near the Chinese Tower.

faq.q: Are Munich's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. They all stand in public parks, squares and streets with no entry fee, though the Nymphenburg palace grounds around one of them charge for the palace interior itself.

trees.name: The Röth-Linde

best_time.label: June and July, when its flowers scent the whole meadow

trees.story: A painter made this tree famous by sitting under it, and the tree has been fighting for its life ever since. Local tradition holds that the linden was planted as a peace tree after the Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, which would put its planting in the mid-17th century, though like most trees on this list its exact age rests on estimate rather than a documented planting record. By the time landscape painter Philipp Röth worked in its shade around the turn of the 20th century, the tree was already reckoned to be some 200 years old, and it now carries his name and a memorial plaque. That long life has come at a cost: a botched fungal treatment in the 1980s left the trunk hollow, and the tree today stands on eight metal crown braces and a branch support, watered and pruned as what one local report calls an intensive-care patient. Winter lindens can live a thousand years under good conditions, which makes the Röth-Linde's current state, still leafing out every spring at 23 metres tall with a trunk over six metres around, as much a story about arboriculture as about age.
trees.access: Free, public land, viewable from outside Gut Nederling
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Nederlinger Straße bus stop or Moosach S-Bahn station
trees.notes: The Thirty Years' War planting date is local tradition, not a documented record; the 300-350 year range comes from the tree's own Wikipedia entry and matches independently, but no source gives a single precise figure. Photo viewed directly: shows a large, mature, dome-shaped linden standing alone on a grassy plot beside a rural-looking building, consistent with the tree's setting near Gut Nederling. Approved. Cross-checked against an OpenStreetMap node (denotation=natural_monument, name=Röth-Linde) within 5m of this entry's own coordinates: independent confirmation the pin is already right.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by eight metal crown braces holding up a hollow trunk over six metres round, kept alive as what one report calls an intensive-care patient. It stands near Gut Nederling, Moosach.

trees.name: The Krüner Eiche
trees.story: This oak has outlasted the village it once stood outside, the Bavarian duchy that once ruled the land, and most of its own major branches. A 2017 recommendation from the Sendling-Westpark district's citizen assembly, arguing for the tree's protection and continued care, dates it at roughly 600 years old, which would put its origins in the 1420s, a period when Munich was still ruled directly by Wittelsbach dukes and when Duke Albrecht III married in the city in 1436. No source directly connects the tree's planting to that or any specific historical event, so any such link stays unclaimed here. What is documented is more recent damage: three major limbs have been removed over the years and a fourth broke off on its own, thinning a crown that once spread wide with the snake-like, twisting branch pattern typical of very old pedunculate oaks. A new protective fence went up around the trunk in July 2022 to keep the compacted soil at the roots from getting worse. The tree still stands at the eastern corner of the small park that carries its name, a six-century survivor now fenced off from the joggers and dog walkers who pass it daily.

trees.name: The Reichs- und Friedenseiche
trees.story: Twelve thousand schoolchildren planted this oak in one afternoon, or at least watched a handful of their classmates do it. On 1 July 1871, weeks after the peace treaty ending the Franco-Prussian War was signed in Frankfurt, Munich staged a peace festival at the Flaucher meadows along the Isar: a procession of children, city councillors and guests gathered while selected boys and girls set a young oak sapling into the ground. A plaque at the site still reads, in German, Reich and Peace Oak, planted by the youth of the city of Munich on 1 July 1871, making this one of the few trees on this list with an exact, undisputed planting date rather than an estimate. Similar Friedenseichen went into the ground across German cities that year, each one a small piece of civic theatre marking the unification of the German Empire under Kaiser Wilhelm I as much as the peace itself. This one has had a century and a half since to grow into an ordinary, unremarkable-looking oak in a riverside park, its real distinction lying entirely in the date rather than the trunk.

trees.name: The Beech of the Englischer Garten

best_time.label: late October, when its leaves turn copper, older than the park Count Rumford built around it

location.address: Englischer Garten, near Forstweg, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: This beech was already old when the park around it was new. The Englischer Garten was laid out from 1789 on the orders of Elector Karl Theodor, designed by the American-born Sir Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, as one of the first public parks on the European continent, open to everyone rather than reserved for a court. Most of what grows in the park today dates from that design and its later 19th century expansion, but this beech, standing between the Forstweg and Friedrich-Ludwig-von-Sckell-Weg paths near the park's second riding trail, predates the whole project, described in Munich's own natural monument register as over 300 years old and the outstanding tree of its immediate surroundings. That would put its origins in the very early 18th century or before, decades ahead of Rumford's landscaping crews, meaning the park's designers either built around an existing tree or the beech simply outgrew whatever else stood nearby before them. No individual measurement or precise felling-based age exists for it, so the three-century figure is treated here as the registered estimate it is rather than a settled fact.

trees.name: The Twin Elms of the Englischer Garten
trees.age_estimate: undated, described as the oldest elms in the city

location.address: Englischer Garten, near the Chinese Tower, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: Munich's own natural monument register makes a specific, checkable claim about these two trees: no older elms are known anywhere in the city. Standing northwest of the Monopteros temple and southwest of the Chinese Tower, in the busiest part of the Englischer Garten, the pair are European white elms, a species that has fared better against Dutch elm disease than most of its European relatives but is still uncommon at real size in any German city after the epidemic spread through the 20th century. Neither tree carries an individual measured age, so the claim rests on comparison rather than a number, but it is specific and official rather than a vague tourist superlative, made by the same city ordinance that protects 200 trees across Munich by name. Thousands of visitors pass within metres of the two elms every week on their way to the Chinese Tower's beer garden, most without knowing they are walking past the oldest confirmed elms the city can point to.

trees.notes: 'No older elms known in the city area' is the register's own wording, a comparative claim rather than an absolute age; no individual figure exists for either tree. Photo viewed directly: shows a tall, mature tree with a complex, high-branching crown rising above the surrounding autumn canopy in a park setting, consistent with the paired elms. Approved. trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech

best_time.label: October, when its narrow, feathery leaves turn golden bronze

location.address: Englischer Garten, west bank of the Schwabinger Bach near the Chinese Tower, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: The old trees of the Englischer Garten did not survive by luck. The park has been tended by the Bavarian palace administration for more than two hundred years and is protected as a garden monument and a landscape conservation area, which is what kept the growing city from building on it. This beech is on the register for a different reason again: it barely exists anywhere else in Munich. The fern-leaved beech is a naturally occurring form of the common European beech in which the leaves grow narrow, deeply cut and lace-like instead of the usual broad oval, a genetic quirk that occasionally turns up in beech forests and gets propagated deliberately when someone notices it. Munich's specimen, standing west of the administrative building near the Chinese Tower on the bank of the Schwabinger Bach stream, has a trunk 3.67 metres around and is registered by the city specifically for how rare the form is within Munich rather than for size or documented age, unlike most of the natural monuments on this list. From a distance in full leaf it can look almost feathery compared to an ordinary beech standing nearby, a small, deliberate anomaly kept alive in one of the park's quieter corners rather than along its main paths.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Chinesischer Turm bus stop
trees.notes: Protected for rarity of form rather than age; no source gives a planting date or age estimate, so the age range here is a rough guess based on trunk girth rather than a documented figure, flagged accordingly. Photo viewed directly: shows a large dome-shaped beech with a finely textured autumn canopy in a park setting with benches beneath it, consistent with a protected specimen beech. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.4km, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_005 for the independent Monopteros cross-check that validated this same table for its immediate neighbour).
trees.verify_notes: Opening corrected 2026-08-26 at the request of Vera Donata Wesinger, Gartenreferentin of the Bayerische Schlossverwaltung, who was forwarded our outreach by the Englischer Garten administration. Our line said these trees are old 'because they survived', which reads as luck. Her correction: they survived because the Englischer Garten is protected as a Gartendenkmal, has been cared for by the Schlossverwaltung for over 200 years, and sits in a Landschaftsschutzgebiet, which together held off the building interests of the city that grew around it. The custodian of the ground is the better source on why the ground still exists.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by leaves cut narrow, deeply lobed and lace-like instead of broad and oval, looking almost feathery beside an ordinary beech nearby. It stands on the west bank of the Schwabinger Bach, near the Chinese Tower.

trees.name: The Oak of the Dörfchen, Nymphenburg
trees.age_estimate: undated, called unique in size for the city

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, near the Brunnhaus, 80638 München

trees.story: This oak grows in the one part of a royal palace garden built to look like it wasn't designed at all. The Dörfchen, or little village, is a cluster of rustic farm-style buildings inside Nymphenburg Palace Park, built from 1803 as a picturesque contrast to the palace's formal Baroque and later English-landscape grounds surrounding it, complete with a working dairy and a chapel meant to evoke ordinary rural life for an audience that never had to live it. The oak stands near the Brunnhaus, on the way toward the Badenburg pavilion and the park's Großer See lake, and Munich's own natural monument register singles it out as unique in size within the city, a claim about scale rather than age, since no source gives the tree a documented planting date or precise age. What is certain is that it has grown large enough, inside grounds that have been continuously maintained by the Bavarian royal family and its successors since the 17th century, to earn individual legal protection in a park already full of centuries-old formal avenues.

trees.name: The Hackberries of Oskar-von-Miller-Ring
trees.age_estimate: undated, described as an extremely rare species group in the city

location.address: Oskar-von-Miller-Ring, near the Siemens headquarters, Maxvorstadt, 80333 München

trees.story: Eight Mediterranean trees grow on a green strip beside one of Munich's busiest ring roads, in a city more than 500 kilometres north of where the species grows wild. Celtis australis, native across southern Europe and North Africa, is registered by Munich as an extremely rare species within the city area, and this group of eight, standing on a green strip on Oskar-von-Miller-Ring west of the Siemens corporate headquarters, is protected as a natural monument specifically for that rarity rather than for any individual tree's size or age. No source gives the group a planting date, though a stand of eight mature specimens growing together suggests a single deliberate planting rather than volunteers that seeded themselves over time, most likely as an ornamental choice for the street rather than a remnant of anything older. Traffic on the ring road runs past them constantly, an odd setting for what the city's own records treat as a genuine botanical rarity worth the same legal protection as its oldest oaks and lindens.

trees.name: The Japanese Pagoda Tree of Karolinenplatz
trees.age_estimate: undated, protected for rarity of size in the cityscape

best_time.label: August, the quietest month of the year for almost anything else blooming in Munich

trees.story: This tree flowers in August, the quietest month of the year for almost anything else blooming in Munich, and does it well enough into old age that the city has singled it out for legal protection twice over, once for rarity of species and once for its unusual size. Styphnolobium japonicum, despite the common name, is native to China rather than Japan and was introduced to European gardens in the 18th century for exactly this trait: heat tolerance, resistance to drought and pollution, and a late, generous flowering of small cream-white blooms that pollinators rely on after most spring flowerers are finished. Munich's specimen stands on the grounds of the property at Karolinenplatz 2a, part of a formal obelisk square laid out in the early 19th century to commemorate Bavarian soldiers who died in Napoleon's Russian campaign, a considerably more sober origin than the tree growing on it. No source gives the tree a documented planting date, but the city's own register notes its size is rare for the species within Munich's built-up centre, an urban tree doing more than its share of feeding late-summer bees.

trees.name: The Wych Elm of Maximiliansplatz
trees.age_estimate: undated, large specimens rare in the city due to Dutch elm disease
trees.story: Almost every elm this size that once grew in Munich is gone, and that absence is the entire reason this one is protected. Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by bark beetles, swept through European elm populations across the 20th century in repeated waves, and Munich's own natural monument register notes plainly that wych elms of any real size have become rare across the whole city as a result, inner districts included. This one has survived on Maximiliansplatz, a roughly 300 by 60 metre park-like square laid out in the English-garden style along what was once the city's western fortification line, redesigned into a green public space after the walls came down in the 19th century. No source gives the tree an individual planting date or precise age, and its story here is less about a specific event than about what elm disease has quietly removed from cities across the continent: a species that was once an unremarkable street and park tree is now something Munich has to name and legally protect just to keep a mature specimen standing.

trees.notes: No individual age or planting date documented; rarity is explicitly tied to Dutch elm disease losses across the city rather than this tree's own age. trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Badenburg
trees.age_estimate: undated, protected for its size and its setting beside the Badenburg

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before darkening

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, about 25 m south of the Badenburg, 80638 München

trees.story: Every copper beech in Europe descends from an accident. The purple leaf is a mutation that appears rarely and at random in wild green beech forests, and every ornamental one since has been propagated by gardeners who found the freak worth keeping. This one stands about 25 metres south of the Badenburg, the bathing pavilion Joseph Effner built for Elector Max Emanuel between 1718 and 1721 around what is generally reckoned the first heated indoor pool built in Europe since Roman times. Munich's natural monument ordinance protects the tree as a solitary specimen and gives its relationship with that building as the reason, which is a statute saying out loud that where a tree stands can matter as much as how big it is. Local descriptions of the park rank it among the mightiest beeches anywhere in the city. Its age is not documented anywhere. What is documented is the ground: Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell converted these grounds from a French baroque garden into an English landscape park between 1799 and 1823, which is when most of the park's free-standing specimen trees were placed, so a planting inside that window is plausible without being proven. Come in late April and the new leaves open a bright translucent red, darkening to near black by August.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 20 min walk west through the park
trees.notes: Age undated: Munich's Naturdenkmal ordinance carries no age or girth column, and no second source gives this tree a date, so the 150-250 range is inferred from Sckell's documented 1799-1823 landscape redesign rather than measured. Existence, species, location and protection are legally attested by the 2021 ordinance; ownership is Freistaat Bayern, public parkland. Flagged because the ordinance is effectively the only source on the tree itself. Photo viewed directly at 1280px before approval: daylight, colour, deep blue sky, the dark purple crown unmistakable against the green trees beside it, trunk visible at the base, and the yellow baroque Badenburg in frame at left, which corroborates the register's stated Badenburg connection. trees.name: The Leaning Lime of the Badenburger See
trees.age_estimate: undated in the city register; a tree-recorders' database estimates roughly 180 years

best_time.label: midwinter, when the leaves drop and the whole leaning frame shows over the ice

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, about 50 m northwest of the Badenburg on the lake shore, 80638 München

trees.story: Munich protects this lime, in law, for being strange looking. The reason recorded in the city's natural monument ordinance is bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, together with a striking appearance, which is an unusually candid thing for a protection statute to say about a tree. It earns it. The trunk leans hard out over the Badenburger See and the whole crown follows, throwing its heaviest limbs sideways across the water rather than upward, so the tree reads as a single long gesture toward the lake. A bench sits underneath, facing the Monopteros on the far shore. A German tree-recorders' database measured the trunk at 4.2 metres around in 2014 and the height at 19 metres, and estimates the tree at about 180 years, which would place its planting inside Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell's conversion of these grounds into an English landscape park between 1799 and 1823. That figure is a volunteer estimate rather than an official one, and the city's own register gives no age at all. Come in winter and the case for the tree is at its clearest: bare, every crooked limb legible against the sky, the lake frozen behind it and the pavilion small and white in the distance.

trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Amalienburg
trees.age_estimate: undated in the city register; a tree-recorders' database estimates roughly 180 years

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, at the path fork about 50 m south of the Amalienburg, 80638 München

trees.story: No fern-leaved beech anywhere is much more than two centuries old, because the tree did not exist before about 1804. It is a cultivated form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow ribbons, and it cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every one of them has been grafted or struck from cuttings taken off another. That gives this specimen an unusually hard ceiling on its age, which is useful in a park where almost nothing else has a date. It stands alone at a fork in the path about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, the rococo hunting lodge Francois de Cuvillies built in the 1730s, with a small metal plate on the trunk marking it as a natural monument. Munich's ordinance calls it a mighty and rare solitary specimen in a good position, and a German tree-recorders' database measured it in 2019 at 2.95 metres around and 25 metres tall, estimating roughly 180 years and recording its condition as vital. Look closely at the foliage and the trick of the tree becomes clear: most of the leaves are shredded to threads, but a branch here and there reverts and throws out ordinary broad beech leaves instead.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 10 min walk west through the park
trees.notes: Named 'of the Amalienburg' deliberately: muc_006 is already 'The Fern-leaved Beech', in the Englischer Garten, and two entries cannot share a name. Same species, different tree, roughly 7 km apart. The 180-year figure and the vitality note come from baumkunde.de register entry 4055, a community-compiled German register, used as a lead and attributed in the story rather than treated as authority; the city ordinance carries no age column. Its coordinates (48.15538, 11.50030) fall about 15 m from the ordinance's, independently corroborating the pin, and its 2019 condition note is the only vitality evidence available for any tree in this cluster. Photo viewed directly at 1280px before approval: daylight, colour, the tree fills the frame with the smooth silvery trunk running the full height and the finely cut foliage readable, path and boulders at the base for scale. Survives a wide card crop, trunk squarely in the centre band. Approved.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by leaves shredded into narrow ribbons, with the odd branch reverting to ordinary broad beech leaves, standing alone at a path fork. It stands about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, Schlosspark Nymphenburg.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Schwanenbrücke

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, south of the Schwanenbrücke, 80638 München

trees.story: Munich protects this beech partly because people are fond of it. The reason entered in the city's natural monument ordinance is that it is a dominant tree in a historic garden with besondere Bedeutung für Münchner Bürger, particular significance for the citizens of Munich, which is a legal document recording public affection as grounds for protection. That is rarer than it sounds; most entries on the same list argue from size, rarity or townscape effect. The tree stands just south of the Schwanenbrücke, the swan bridge over the canal that runs north through the park. A weeping beech grows nothing like the wild form it was bred from: instead of a clean grey column carrying a high crown, the limbs arch outward and then fall, so the branches hang to the ground and the whole tree closes around a hollow space at its centre. Walking under one is the point of it, and generations of Munich children have done exactly that here. Its age is not recorded anywhere. The cultivar has only been in general garden circulation since the early nineteenth century, and the surrounding park was landscaped between 1799 and 1823, which brackets it loosely and honestly without pretending to a date.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 15 min walk northwest through the park
trees.notes: Age undated and no second source beyond the ordinance itself, so flagged. The 120-200 range is bracketed from the cultivar's introduction date and Sckell's 1799-1823 landscaping, not measured; baumkunde.de has no entry for this tree. Photo deliberately left missing rather than filled. Three candidates exist on Wikimedia Commons and all three were checked: the register-linked 'Haengebuche im Schlosspark Nymphenburg.jpg' was viewed directly at 1280px and fails the Cadiz standard, being a close-up shot looking up into the canopy with no trunk base, no whole-tree shape and no sense of scale, plus a painted red heart on one limb; the other two ('Unter der Haengebuche', 'Laub der Haengebuche') are by the same photographer and are respectively an under-canopy and a foliage close-up, failing the same way. An honest gap beats a mediocre photo. Worth re-hunting when someone photographs this tree whole.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the beech whose limbs arch out and fall to the ground, closing around a hollow space you can walk into. It stands just south of the Schwanenbrücke, Schlosspark Nymphenburg.

trees.name: The White Ash of Maximiliansplatz
trees.story:
There is an American ash on a square in central Munich, and the city's own ordinance calls the species rare here.

Fraxinus americana is the wood a classic baseball bat is turned from, straight-grained, light and good at absorbing shock. In Europe it is a park curiosity rather than a forest tree, which is why Munich's protection order gives as its reason: dominant tree with an interesting growth form, rare in Munich. It stands in the green strip at Maximiliansplatz, in the middle of the city, free to walk up to.

Ashes have become a heavier thing to look at over the past two decades. A fungus called ash dieback has been working through Europe's native ash since the 1990s and has killed a large share of it, while the American species is under siege at home from the emerald ash borer, a beetle that has taken tens of millions of trees across North America. A big ash of any species with its crown in good order is no longer an ordinary sight.

Its age is simply unknown: the city's list records why a tree is protected and not when it was planted, and no dated source was found. Ash comes into leaf later and drops earlier than most of what surrounds it, so it spends more of the year bare than its neighbours do.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the American ash on the green strip, a species Munich calls rare here, with a crown that comes into leaf later and drops earlier than its neighbours. It stands on the green strip at Maximiliansplatz.

trees.name: The Lime of the Englischer Garten
trees.story:
This lime is already drawn on a plan of the park from 1807, which makes it one of very few trees in Munich with a paper trail.

Munich's protection ordinance says so in as many words: historic lime, already present in plans from the year 1807. Read that as a floor rather than an age. A tree worth drawing was not a sapling, so it was standing when Bavaria was a kingdom barely a year old and when the Englischer Garten itself was under twenty years into its existence. The park had been laid out from 1789 on the orders of Elector Karl Theodor, at the urging of Benjamin Thompson, and was unusual in Europe for being open to everyone rather than to a court.

What the tree has watched since is the whole modern history of the city, from the first generation of Müncheners allowed to walk in a royal park to whoever is crossing the meadow this afternoon.

Beyond that 1807 drawing there is no age and no girth on record, so anything more precise would be invention. Large-leaved lime flowers in June, ahead of the other European limes, and an old one like this holds a broad, heavy, slightly lopsided crown that reads as a single dome from right across the grass.

photo.note: Weeping willows by a stream, not a lime.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, broad and heavy and slightly lopsided, reading as a single dome from right across the grass. It stands in the Englischer Garten, and it flowers in June, ahead of the other European limes.

trees.name: The Beech of the Flaucheranlagen
trees.story:
Munich's ordinance calls this one of the mightiest beeches in the city and notes that it carries branches almost to the ground.

The second half of that is the part to hold on to. A beech grown in a wood loses its lower limbs to shade and ends up a smooth grey column with all its leaves fifteen metres overhead. A beech grown in the open keeps everything, and the crown comes down in a skirt you have to duck under to reach the trunk. This one has had the room to do it, in the Flaucher, the belt of riverside park along the Isar in the south of the city where Munich goes to swim and grill through the summer.

The river beside it is not the one it grew up with. Straightened and walled in the nineteenth century, the stretch through the city was rebuilt between 2000 and 2011, the concrete lifted out and gravel banks let back in, so the beech now stands over a braided river rather than a channel.

The city's list gives the reason for protection and no dimensions, so there is no published age or girth. From late October the whole crown turns copper and holds it for weeks, and beech is stubborn about letting go: the young growth keeps its dead leaves all winter.

best_time.label: late October into November, when a crown this size turns the whole clearing copper

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches, which come almost to the ground in a skirt you have to duck under to reach the trunk. It stands in the Flaucher, the riverside park along the Isar in the south of the city.

trees.name: The Small-leaved Lime of the Englischer Garten
trees.story:
For centuries in this part of Europe, a village's justice was handed down under a lime.

The Gerichtslinde, the court lime, was a real institution: a broad tree on the square with benches beneath it, where the local court sat in the open because everybody could then see and hear what had been decided. Small-leaved lime was usually the tree chosen, because it lives long, takes heavy pruning and builds exactly that kind of wide, shading crown. Munich protects this one for its trunk, which the ordinance describes as having rarity value in the city on account of its form and its girth. It stands on open ground in the Englischer Garten.

That girth is never given a number. The city's list says why a tree is protected and stops there, so the trunk that earned this tree its protection has no published measurement and no date beside it.

Small-leaved lime flowers later than any other European lime, in late June and July, once most of the summer's blossom is over. The flowers themselves are small, greenish and easy to walk past. You will not walk past the sound, because the whole crown fills with bees, and the scent reaches you a good twenty metres before the tree does.

best_time.label: late June into July, when it flowers late for a lime and the crown fills with bees

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a wide, heavily pruned crown built for shade, the type of lime once used as a village court tree, standing on open ground. It stands in the Englischer Garten.

trees.name: The Norway Maple of Herrnstraße

best_time.label: April, when it flowers before it leafs and the bare crown turns acid yellow-green

trees.story:
Munich protects this maple for being big, which says more about the species than about the tree. Acer platanoides is among the most planted street trees in Europe and among the most frequently cut back: fast, cheap, tolerant of road salt, compacted soil and bad air, and generally treated as replaceable. The city's 2021 natural monument ordinance takes the opposite line here, entering it as stadtbildwirksam, effective in the townscape, and rare at this size within the city. That is a statute saying a common tree becomes an uncommon one simply by being left alone.

It stands on Herrnstraße in the Lehel, the grid of tall nineteenth century blocks laid out between the old town wall and the Isar when Munich first built beyond its gates. This is dense inner city: courtyards, parked cars, five storeys on both sides, and one crown holding the middle of it.

If you want to be certain what you are looking at, snap a leaf stalk. A Norway maple bleeds white, and the sycamore it is constantly mistaken for does not. In April it flowers before it leafs, and the bare crown turns acid yellow-green for a fortnight.

The ordinance records why a tree is protected and never when it was planted. No dated source exists for this one, so how long it has stood here is not known.
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Isartor station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by snapping a leaf stalk: a Norway maple bleeds white and the sycamore it gets mistaken for does not. It stands on Herrnstraße in the Lehel, one crown holding the middle of a street five storeys high on both sides.

trees.name: The Beech of the Wilhelmsgymnasium

best_time.label: late October and November, when the crown turns copper over the green in front of the school

trees.story:
The school across this green space has been teaching since 1559, which makes it the oldest in Munich. The beech below it carries no recorded date of any kind, and the city protects it anyway. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance enters it as a mighty, dominant tree, effective in the streetscape, and that is the entire reasoning.

Fagus sylvatica behaves badly in cities, which is why a full grown one in the Lehel is worth the detour. It wants deep, moist, well drained ground, it resents compacted soil, and its bark is thin and smooth enough to scald in full sun where a rough barked oak would shrug. Given room it becomes the most dominant broadleaf in central Europe: the shade under a mature beech is close to total, almost nothing germinates in it, and the floor stays bare leaf litter year after year. That is how the species took most of the continent's forests.

The Wilhelmsgymnasium moved into its building on the corner in 1877, a Jesuit foundation by then three centuries into its second life as a state school. The green strip on its south side is the sort of leftover municipal ground that usually holds bins and a bike rack.

No age is on record. The ordinance lists reasons for protection and carries no column for dates or dimensions, and nothing else has measured this tree.
trees.transport: 1 min walk from the Maxmonument bus stop
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the deep shade: almost nothing germinates under a mature beech, so the floor stays bare leaf litter. It stands in the green strip on the south side of the Wilhelmsgymnasium, in the Lehel.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of St.-Anna-Platz

best_time.label: May, when it puts up white candles over the benches on the square

trees.story:
Munich's beer gardens are chestnut groves for an engineering reason. Brewers dug cellars along the Isar to hold beer through the summer and planted horse chestnuts over them, because the species throws heavy shade from shallow roots that will not force their way into a vault. Then they discovered that people would rather drink under the trees than carry the beer home, and the beer garden existed.

This one shades no cellar. It stands at the southwest corner of St.-Anna-Platz in the Lehel, between two churches of very different temperament: the small Klosterkirche finished in 1733, generally counted the first rococo church built in Old Bavaria, and the far larger parish church that went up beside it in the 1890s. Both were gutted by bombing and rebuilt.

The 2021 natural monument ordinance protects the tree as platzbildprägend, defining the square, and calls it mighty and healthy. Healthy is the word to notice. Since the 1990s the horse chestnut leaf miner, a moth out of the Balkans, has browned and curled the foliage of chestnuts across Europe by mid July, so a chestnut still carrying green leaves in August is doing better than most of its species.

Its age is not on record anywhere. The ordinance gives reasons and no dates, and nothing else has measured this tree.
trees.transport: 1 min walk from Lehel station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, still green in August when the leaf miner has browned most chestnuts in Europe. It stands at the southwest corner of St.-Anna-Platz, between the small Klosterkirche and the larger parish church.

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Luitpoldpark
trees.story:
The hill in this park is what was left of Munich after 1945. From 1946 onward the rubble of the bombed city was carted up to Schwabing and piled into the Luitpoldhügel, roughly 37 metres of broken masonry now buried under grass and footpaths, with a view across to the Olympic Park from the top.

The park underneath it is older. It was laid out in 1911, when 90 lime trees went in for the ninetieth birthday of Prince Regent Luitpold. The hackberry is not one of them. Celtis australis belongs to southern Europe, Asia Minor and North Africa, its natural range stopping well south of the Alps, and Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance calls it an extremely rare species in the city, protected here for being beautiful and for an interesting growth form rather than for any size.

It was the timber of whip handles, pitchforks and walking sticks, chosen because it bends a long way before it breaks. The quickest way to be sure you have found one is the leaf: lopsided at the base, one half running further down the stalk than the other, with a hard toothed edge. The fruit is a small dark drupe, sweet and almost entirely stone.

The ordinance records why the tree is protected, never when it was planted, and no age exists for it anywhere.
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Scheidplatz station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a lopsided leaf base, one half running further down the stalk than the other, standing apart from the park's 1911 lime plantings. It stands in the Luitpoldpark.

trees.name: The Amur Cork Tree of the Luitpoldpark
trees.story:
You can press a thumb into this tree and the bark gives. The Amur cork tree carries a thick, soft, deeply ridged corky layer that dents under a hand and springs back, which is exactly why Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it for an interesting bark pattern and calls the species extremely rare in the city.

Phellodendron amurense comes from the Amur river country on the Russian and Chinese border, and from Korea and northern Japan, which is a continental climate with harder winters than Bavaria has ever managed. Under the cork the inner bark is a startling sulphur yellow, and it is one of the fundamental herbs of Chinese medicine. The leaves are pinnate, like an ash, and turn clear yellow in autumn; the berries are black and smell of turpentine when crushed. In the northeastern United States the same tree seeds itself so aggressively into hardwood forest that several states have banned its sale. In a Schwabing park it just stands there being unusual.

The ground it stands on is the Luitpoldpark, laid out in 1911 and dominated by a hill made from the rubble of the bombed city. A Mediterranean hackberry, protected under the same ordinance for the same rarity, grows about 200 metres east.

The ordinance lists reasons and carries no dates or measurements, so the tree's age is unknown.
trees.transport: 3 min walk from the Ackermannstraße tram stop
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by thick, deeply ridged corky bark that dents under a thumb and springs back, its inner bark a startling sulphur yellow beneath. It stands in the Luitpoldpark, about 200 metres from the park's protected hackberry.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Gasteig

best_time.label: September and October, when the conkers ripen and drop along the pavement

trees.story:
Gasteig comes from gacher Steig, steep path, and that is the whole explanation of this corner of Munich. The ground drops away here to the Isar, so everything on the slope has had to be terraced, buttressed or built into the bank, and the horse chestnut stands at the top of the fall. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a striking, wide-spreading tree, particularly effective in the streetscape.

Wide-spreading is the phrase worth stopping on. A street chestnut is normally cut back into a lollipop to keep it clear of the trams, the wires and the upper windows, and it spends its life as half a crown. This one has been left to throw its lower limbs out sideways, which is what the species does when nobody interferes.

Its neighbour is the Gasteig itself, the concert hall that opened in 1985 as home of the Munich Philharmonic and emptied out in 2021 for a rebuild, the orchestra decamping to a converted industrial hall across the river. The tree stayed where it was.

The species is not local either. Aesculus hippocastanum is native to a handful of mountain ravines in Greece and Albania, where it is a threatened tree, and planted by the million everywhere else. No age is recorded here: Munich's ordinance says why a tree is protected and never how old it is.
trees.transport: 1 min walk from the Am Gasteig tram stop
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lower limbs thrown out sideways, where the street chestnuts around it are cut back into lollipops. It stands at the top of the slope down to the Isar, beside the Gasteig concert hall.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Edlingerstraße

best_time.label: May, when the whole dome goes up in white candles

trees.story:
The word Munich's ordinance uses for this tree is Solitär, which in the trade means a tree with open ground on every side and therefore the shape the species actually has. Almost no street tree gets that. They go in as rows, get pruned away from windows and cables, and end up as half a crown facing the road. This chestnut got the room, and the 2021 natural monument ordinance says as much: a solitary, beautiful and evenly grown tree, very dominant in the streetscape.

It stands where Sommerstraße meets Edlingerstraße in the Au, the low quarter on the flood plain of the Isar that spent centuries being washed out by the river and just as long being the poorest district in Munich. A few streets away, Mariahilfplatz has hosted the Auer Dult three times a year since 1905, a crockery and junk fair whose market privileges run back to the eighteenth century.

An evenly grown horse chestnut is a specific thing to stand under: a dome that starts low and closes to a point, carried on limbs that sweep down before turning back up at the tips. In May the whole of it goes up in white candles, each flower marked with a yellow blotch that turns red once it has been pollinated, so the tree is telling the bees which ones are already finished.

No age is on record.
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Kolumbusplatz station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a horse chestnut given open ground on every side, growing into a full dome rather than the half-crown most street trees end up with. It stands where Sommerstraße meets Edlingerstraße, in the Au.

trees.name: The Downy Birch of the Flaucher
trees.story:
Downy birch is the last broadleaved tree before the tundra. Betula pubescens grows further north than any other, past the Arctic Circle in Scandinavia and across Iceland, and it manages it by staying quick, modest and short lived; a hundred years is a long run for one. Which makes Munich's reason for protecting this one worth reading twice: a mighty solitary tree, rare at this size in the city.

It stands in the Flaucher, the belt of gravel banks, pine and poplar along the Isar in the south of Munich where the city comes to swim and grill from May to September. That is the right ground for it. This is the wet-footed birch, the one that takes bogs, fens and river gravel where the silver birch cannot follow, and the fine hairs on its young twigs, the pubescens of the name, are how the two are told apart.

Birch bark is white for the same reason a roof is painted white. Betulin, the compound that makes the papery outer layer, reflects sunlight and keeps the trunk from warming and then splitting on cold bright days. It also burns when soaking wet, which is why birch bark has been lighting fires across northern Europe for as long as there have been fires to light.

The ordinance gives the reason for protection and no dimensions and no date, and nothing else has measured the tree.
trees.transport: 7 min walk from the Tierpark (Alemannenstraße) bus stop
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fine hairs on its young twigs, which is what separates a downy birch from a silver, and by the white trunk. It stands alone among the pine and poplar on the Isar gravel in the Flaucher.

trees.name: The Ash of Leinthalerstraße
trees.story:
Munich's ordinance gives three words for why this tree is protected: extrem ausladende Krone, an extremely wide-spreading crown. No size, no age, no history, nothing about the street. Just the shape, and it was enough.

The shape is also evidence. Fraxinus excelsior grown in a wood goes up tall and narrow, drawn on by its neighbours, and it only spreads when there is nothing beside it to compete with. A crown wide enough to earn a protection order on its own is a crown that grew in the open, and Freimann was farmland and village until Munich absorbed it in 1931. An ash does not spread like that in a street.

Ash is also the tree Europe is currently losing. A fungus from east Asia, harmless to the ashes it evolved alongside, reached Poland in the early 1990s and has been killing European ash ever since, blackening the leaves and thinning the crown from the top down. Some trees resist it and nobody yet knows how many, so a mature ash still carrying a full crown is not the ordinary sight it was thirty years ago.

The ordinance carries no dates and no measurements, and nothing else has recorded this tree, so its age is unknown. What is on the record is that in a list full of mighty and dominant trees, this one got in on width alone.
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Freimann station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, extremely wide-spreading where a woodland ash goes up tall and narrow. It stands on the corner of Leinthalerstraße and Sondermeierstraße in Freimann.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Situlistraße
trees.story:
By the city's own reckoning this is the largest weeping beech standing in Munich. The 2021 natural monument ordinance says so in its reason for protection, hedged with derzeit, currently, which is the honest way to make a superlative about something alive.

Every weeping beech is a graft. Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula' does not come true from seed, so each one is a cutting from the same weeping line joined onto the roots of an ordinary green beech, and on older specimens the union often still shows as a change in the bark near the ground. Above it the tree does what no wild beech does. The limbs arch outward and then fall, layer over layer, until the branch tips reach the ground and the whole crown closes into a room. Getting inside and standing at the trunk is the point of the species, and the reason gardeners have kept grafting it since the early nineteenth century.

It grows in the grounds at Situlistraße 73-75 in Freimann, about 70 metres from a copper beech the same ordinance protects on its own account, so the two are one short walk rather than two errands.

No age is recorded. The ordinance names reasons and never dates, so the city has written down that this is the biggest of its kind here without recording a single number about it.
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Freimann station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branch tips, which fall all the way to the ground and close the crown into a room you can walk inside. It stands at Situlistraße 73-75, about 70 metres from the protected copper beech.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Situlistraße

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves are thin enough to hold the sun behind them

trees.story:
Purple leaves are a handicap. A copper beech is an ordinary beech carrying a mutation that floods its foliage with anthocyanin, which masks the chlorophyll underneath and cuts the light the leaf can actually put to work. In a wild forest that is a losing hand: purple seedlings are outgrown by green ones and vanish. The tree only exists in numbers because gardeners liked the colour and kept propagating what the forest would have discarded.

This is the second protected beech at Situlistraße 73-75 in Freimann. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance lists it separately from the weeping beech about 70 metres away, calling it a dominant tree that defines the local townscape and unique in the area, which for a document that mostly says mighty and dominant counts as enthusiasm.

What the ordinance does not list is a date, a girth or a height. It records reasons for protection and nothing else, and no other source has measured this tree, so the beech is documented in law and entirely undated.

The handicap gets paid off for about a fortnight a year. The new leaves open in late April and early May a thin luminous red you can see the sun through, then thicken and darken all summer towards something close to black. In August it is the heaviest looking thing on the street. In May it is the brightest.
trees.transport: 4 min walk from the Kulturheimstraße bus stop
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the purple leaves, red and translucent when they open in late April and close to black by August. It stands at Situlistraße 73-75, about 70 metres from the weeping beech the city protects separately.

trees.name: The Lime of the Porcelain Manufactory
trees.story:
A small-leaved lime grows on the working grounds of the Nymphenburg Porcelain Manufactory, Bavaria's royal china works, founded in 1747 and still hand-painting porcelain in the same rondell building today. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects the tree for being dominant and shaping the townscape, the same reasoning it gives dozens of trees across the city, and a local paper listed it among eleven giants declared natural monuments in 2011.

The Nördliches Schlossrondell is one of two crescent buildings curving out from the forecourt of Nymphenburg Palace, built to house the court's workshops rather than its aristocracy. Porcelain has fired here since the manufactory moved onto the grounds in 1761, through a change from crown property to the family firm that runs it now.

The lime stands close enough to the palace park's other protected trees, an oak, a beech and two more limes half a kilometre south, to make a short walk of it. Nobody has dated it. If you have stood under it, or work in the manufactory and can ask, tell us.
verified_sources: Wochenanzeiger München, 12 Oct 2011, 'Mächtig, hoch und dominant': eleven trees declared Naturdenkmal in the city's western districts, naming this lime at Nördliches Schlossrondell 8
trees.access: Free, on the grounds of the Nymphenburg Porcelain Manufactory; open during shop hours, Monday to Friday 10:00-18:30, Saturday 10:00-16:00, closed Sunday and public holidays.
trees.transport: Tram 12, 16 or 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, a couple of minutes' walk

photo.attribution: Peterf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime growing on the working grounds of the Nymphenburg Porcelain Manufactory, close enough to the palace park's other protected trees for a short walk between them. It stands at Nördliches Schlossrondell 8.

trees.name: The Sycamore Maple of Theresienstraße
trees.story:
A mountain tree ended up on a flat city street and outgrew everything on it. Sycamore maples belong to the Alps and the uplands of central Europe, where they root in steep pasture and broken rock; this one stands on the gravel plain the Isar laid down, on Theresienstrasse in Maxvorstadt. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it in one line, and that line is a compliment rather than a measurement: a strikingly handsome, dominantly grown tree, effective in the streetscape.

Maxvorstadt was Munich's first planned expansion beyond the medieval walls, a grid drawn from 1805 and now the quarter of the university and the Pinakotheken. Theresienstrasse runs east to west through the middle of it, a long straight of shopfronts, institutes and parked bicycles, and the maple is the one thing on its stretch with a crown worth standing under.

Nobody has put a date on it. The ordinance keeps no age column and no girth column, and no other source names this tree, so all that is on record is that the city looked at it and decided it was worth keeping. If you know when it went in, or have taken a tape around the trunk, tell us and we will add it.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one tree on this stretch of shopfronts and institutes with a crown worth standing under, a mountain species out of place on a flat gravel plain. It stands at Theresienstraße 90, Maxvorstadt.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Gollierplatz
trees.story:
Munich's beer gardens are shaded by this species for an engineering reason. Brewers dug ice cellars along the Isar terraces and planted horse chestnuts over the vaults, because the roots run shallow and do no damage below while the leaves throw a dense, low shade that kept the beer cold through August. The tree came from the mountains of the Balkans and reached central Europe in the sixteenth century as a curiosity; Bavaria put it to work.

This one is off duty. It stands on Gollierplatz, the green square at the heart of the Westend, and Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a wide-spreading tree that stands out clearly above the others around it. That is worth knowing before you go, because the square has plenty of trees and only one of them is the one you came for: look for the crown that overtops the rest.

The Westend is a dense grid of tenement blocks thrown up for workers at the end of the nineteenth century, on the rise just above the Theresienwiese, where the Oktoberfest has been held since 1810. Gollierplatz is where the quarter goes to sit down.

The city recorded no age for it and nobody else has published one. If you know the square's history, or the tree's, we would like to hear it.
trees.transport: In Schwanthalerhöhe, close to the Gollierplatz tram stop

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a crown that overtops every other tree on the square, the one to look for among several. It stands on Gollierplatz, in the Westend.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Hartmannshofer Park
trees.story:
Munich's protection order calls this tree rare, which is an odd thing to say about a red oak. The species is everywhere in European parks: brought over from eastern North America in the eighteenth century for fast timber and for the autumn colour, and planted by the thousand ever since. What is rare is one allowed to reach full size inside a city. The ordinance says so in five words of German that translate as a very large red oak, rare within the city, and leaves it there.

It stands in Hartmannshofer Park in Moosach, in Munich's north-west, on ground that was estate land before the city reached it. Red oak leaves are the giveaway: big, thin, with bristle tips on each lobe, nothing like the round-lobed native oaks, and in autumn the whole crown goes scarlet rather than the brown that a pedunculate oak settles for. The bark stays smooth and grey far longer than a European oak's, which is another way to be sure you are standing at the right trunk.

No age is recorded anywhere. Red oaks grow fast, so size is a poor guide here, and guessing would be worse than admitting it. If you know when this one was planted, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the crown turns scarlet

trees.transport: In Moosach's Hartmannshofer Park
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, each lobe ending in a bristle where Munich's native oaks are round, and by the bark, smooth and grey far longer than theirs. It stands in Hartmannshofer Park in Moosach.

trees.name: The White Willow of the Isar Floodplain

location.address: Isar riverside path, left bank north of the Großlappen treatment works, 80995 München

trees.story:
A white willow is normally one of a crowd. It is the pioneer of the gravel bar, the first thing to root after a flood has scoured the bank, and it grows in thickets because that is how the river plants it. This one grew up alone, and Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it for exactly that: a mighty, solitary and striking tree, rare within the city at this size.

It stands on the left bank of the Isar in the northern floodplain beyond Freimann, where the river is still allowed to sprawl across shingle and side channels instead of running between engineered banks. The German name for the species is Silberweide, silver willow, and on a windy day you see why: the leaves are white underneath, so a gust turns the whole crown pale in one movement. Nothing else on the riverside path does that.

Willows put on wood fast and hollow out early, which means girth says very little about years here. The city recorded no age, no other source names this tree, and any number we offered would be arithmetic dressed up as a fact. If you have measured it, or watched it through a few floods, we would rather have your account than our guess. The riverside path runs past it and is open all year.
trees.transport: On the public Isar riverside path in the northern floodplain, Freimann
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in the wind: the leaves are white underneath, so a gust turns the whole crown pale, and nothing else on the path does that. It stands alone on the riverside path, left bank of the Isar.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Kirchtruderinger Straße
trees.story:
If you find this chestnut brown and blotched in August, autumn has nothing to do with it. Since the 1990s a small moth, the horse chestnut leaf miner, has spread across central Europe and mines the leaves of nearly every chestnut on the continent, browning them weeks early. The tree survives it and keeps flowering; it simply stops looking its best at the exact moment people are out in shirtsleeves. Come in May instead, when the candles are up and the leaf miners have not yet got going.

What brought it onto Munich's protected list is bulk. The 2021 ordinance calls it a mighty free-standing tree, rare within the city at this size, and free-standing is the operative word: no neighbours, no competition, a full dome from the ground up. It stands on Kirchtruderinger Strasse, the road named for the church end of Trudering, a farming village east of Munich that had its own parish long before the city grew out to meet it and swallowed it whole.

The register carries no age and nobody else has published one, which is normal for a street tree that was never famous. Trudering keeps its own local history well. If somebody there knows when this chestnut was planted, we would like to put the year on the page.
trees.transport: In Trudering, a few minutes from Trudering S-Bahn station

best_time.label: May, when it flowers

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the shape, a full dome from the ground up with no neighbours to crowd it. It stands alone on Kirchtruderinger Straße, the road named for the church end of Trudering.

trees.name: The Beech of Kagerstraße
trees.story:
A beech that still has its lowest branches has never had a neighbour. In a beech wood the low limbs die in the shade of the canopy and drop off, which is why forest beeches stand like grey columns with nothing on them for the first ten metres. An even crown that sweeps all the way down to the grass is the shape of a tree that grew up in the open with all the light to itself, and that is precisely what Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance records here: a large solitary tree with an even crown reaching down to the ground.

It stands on Kagerstrasse in Ramersdorf-Perlach, in the south-east of the city, on the sort of residential street where a tree this size is the only thing older than the houses. Fagus sylvatica is the species that would cover most of central Europe if we left it alone, and it casts the deepest shade of any tree here, which is why almost nothing grows underneath one.

The city recorded no age and no girth, and no second source names it, so the honest answer is that nobody has dated it. If somebody on Kagerstrasse remembers the tree from childhood, or has put a tape around the trunk, that is already more than any register holds.

best_time.label: late October and November, when the copper runs from the top of the crown down to the grass

trees.transport: In Ramersdorf-Perlach, on Kagerstraße
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the even crown, which sweeps all the way down to the grass where a forest beech would be bare for its first ten metres. It stands alone on Kagerstraße in Ramersdorf-Perlach.

trees.name: The Hornbeam of Wilrampark

location.address: Wilrampark, south of the playground, 81929 München

trees.story:
Hornbeam is the hardest wood in the European forest, and it was never meant to become a tree like this. Carpenters cut it for the parts that had to survive being hit: mill cogs, the teeth of wooden gearwheels, butchers' blocks, ox yokes. It blunts tools and it burns hotter than oak. The English name says as much twice over, horn for hardness and beam for tree. A wood that useful was normally coppiced or laid into a hedge and cut back every few years, which is why a full-grown solitary hornbeam is a scarce thing.

This one was left alone, and Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a solitary tree with an even crown, rare in Munich at this size. It stands in Wilrampark in Ramersdorf-Perlach, just south of the playground, which makes it easy to find and easy to sit under. Look at the trunk rather than the crown: hornbeam grows fluted, with muscular vertical ridges running up it like tensed sinew, and nothing else in the park has that surface.

No age is on record, here or anywhere else, and the city register keeps no girth column either. If you have put a tape around this trunk, we would like the number for the page.
trees.transport: In Wilrampark, Ramersdorf-Perlach
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, fluted into muscular vertical ridges that nothing else in the park has. It stands in Wilrampark, just south of the playground.

trees.name: The Norway Maple of Mondstraße
trees.story:
Snap a leaf stalk off this tree and it bleeds white. That milky sap is the one reliable way to tell a Norway maple from the sycamore maples it otherwise resembles, and it is the sort of trick worth knowing at a trunk where the leaves are twenty metres up. What you can see from the pavement is scale: Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance calls it a very mighty, singular tree that defines the square it stands in, which is a lot of authority to hand one maple.

The square is on Mondstrasse in Untergiesing, moon street, on the low ground by the Isar below the terrace that Giesing proper sits on. Giesing was a poor quarter of brickworkers and day labourers long before it was a fashionable one, and its street corners are small, hard and short of green. A tree that determines what one of them looks like is doing real work.

Norway maple is the first of the big shade trees to flower here, in April, in acid yellow-green clusters that open before the leaves and are easy to mistake for early foliage from a distance.

The register records no age, and no other source names this tree. If you have a date for it, send it over.

best_time.label: October, when the crown turns clear butter yellow over the square

trees.transport: In Untergiesing-Harlaching, on Mondstraße
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by white sap bleeding from a snapped leaf stalk, the trick that tells it apart from a sycamore maple, and by a crown large enough to define the whole square. It stands on Mondstraße, Untergiesing.

trees.name: The Ash of Bleibtreuplatz
trees.story:
Europe is losing its ash trees, so a big one with a full crown is worth going to look at while it is there. A fungus from east Asia turned up in eastern Europe in the early 1990s, spread across the continent within two decades and has killed ash on a scale that has changed what woods look like in a single human lifetime. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance says nothing about any of that. It protects this tree in seven words: a mighty tree with a wide, funnel-shaped crown.

Funnel is the right word for a healthy ash. The limbs leave the trunk at a narrow angle and then swing outward and up, so the whole thing opens like a wide beaker rather than spreading like an oak. Dieback shows in the opposite direction, as thinning from the top down and dead twig ends against the sky, which makes this a tree you can assess for yourself in a few seconds from the pavement.

It stands on Bleibtreuplatz in Solln, a villa suburb of large gardens and quiet corners in Munich's south-west. Nobody has published an age for it. If you pass it often and notice the crown thinning, or if you know when it was planted, tell us and we will update the page.
trees.transport: In Solln, on Bleibtreuplatz
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, wide and funnel-shaped: the limbs leave the trunk at a narrow angle and then swing out and up like a beaker. It stands on Bleibtreuplatz in Solln.

trees.name: The Lime of the Muttenthaler Pond
trees.story:
The best part of this lime is at the bottom. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance gives most trees on its list one clause about size or crown; this one gets a note about its feet, praising a pronounced, wide, chalice-shaped stem base along with the presence it has in the landscape beside the pond. Old limes do that. The trunk flares out at ground level into buttresses that run into the soil like poured wax, and on a big one the flare can be wider than a person can reach around.

It grows at the water on Muttenthalerstrasse in Solln, at the south-western edge of Munich, where the streets are wide and the gardens are old. A lime and a pond is not an accidental combination in Bavaria. The linden was the tree villages planted where they met, danced and held court, and water and a bench tend to follow the same logic.

Go and stand at the base rather than photographing the crown from across the water, because the base is what the city singled out. Age is the one thing missing: the register has no year and no girth for it, and no second source names the tree at all. Anyone with a tape measure can tell us more than the paperwork does.
trees.transport: In Solln, beside the pond on Muttenthalerstraße
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk base flaring out into wide, chalice-shaped buttresses at ground level, wider than the crown above suggests. It stands at the pond on Muttenthalerstraße, Solln.

trees.name: The Ash of Pasinger Stadtpark
trees.story:
This ash branches low, and for an ash that is unusual enough to be the reason it is protected. Grown in a wood, Fraxinus excelsior runs straight up as a clean pole and puts its crown out at the top where the light is; foresters like it for exactly that. This one carries a mighty crown set low on the trunk, which is how Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance describes it, along with the way it dominates the landscape around it. It means the branches are within sight rather than overhead, and the tree reads as a shape rather than a column.

It stands in Pasinger Stadtpark, the park strung along the Wurm on its way north out of Lake Starnberg, ten minutes on foot from Pasing station. The ash is worth timing: it is the last big tree in the park to come into leaf, often not until well into May, and among the first to drop, which gives it a shorter summer than anything standing next to it. In winter you can pick it out by the buds, matt black and blunt, unlike any other tree here.

The register carries no age or girth for it and no second source names it, so its years are an open question. Answers welcome.
trees.transport: In Pasinger Stadtpark, a short walk from Pasing station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown set low on the trunk, and in winter by the buds, matt black and blunt where nothing else in the park has them. It stands in Pasinger Stadtpark, by the Wurm.

trees.name: The Lime of Landsberger Straße
trees.story:
Landsberger Strasse is the old road west out of Munich, the one that ran to Landsberg and on toward Augsburg before anybody thought of a motorway, and near its far end this lime holds down a corner of Pasing. Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a dominant tree that shapes both the street and the town around it, which is a heavy claim to make about one tree on a busy road. It lands differently here than it would elsewhere in the city, because Pasing was a town in its own right before Munich absorbed it. It still has its own Rathaus, its own market and its own centre of gravity, and the lime stands close to all three.

Large-leaved lime is the German town tree by long habit: it takes hard pruning, poor soil and traffic, it throws new shoots from the base when it is cut back, and it can keep that up for centuries. Its leaves are the bigger of the two native limes, soft and faintly hairy underneath, and it flowers a fortnight or so ahead of the small-leaved lime in early summer.

No age has been recorded, by the city or anyone else. Pasing keeps its history close. If a local knows this tree's, we would like to hear it.
trees.transport: In Pasing, on Landsberger Straße near the town hall
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime the city says shapes both the street and the town around it, on the old road that once ran west out of Munich toward Landsberg. It stands at Landsberger Straße 486, Pasing.

trees.name: The Oak of Maria-Eich-Straße
trees.story:
Maria-Eich-Strasse means Mary's Oak Street, and this is not that oak. The name belongs to the pilgrimage site at Planegg, out beyond the city boundary at the far end of the road, where by tradition a figure of the Virgin was set into a hollow oak in the early eighteenth century and a chapel grew up around the spot. Whether the street was named for that tree or simply for the place it leads to, the oak standing on it in Obermenzing today is a separate tree with a separate life, and the city protects it on its own account: a dominant tree that shapes the townscape, in the words of Munich's 2021 natural monument ordinance.

Obermenzing is the green, villa-and-garden neighbour of Pasing in Munich's west, and a pedunculate oak here is a native on home ground rather than an import. Quercus robur is the species that carried central Europe: pigs were driven out to fatten on its acorns, ships and roof beams came out of its timber, and a single mature one supports more insect species than almost any other tree here.

The register gives no age and no girth for it. Oaks reward a tape measure more than most. If you bring one, tell us what you find.
trees.transport: In Obermenzing, on Maria-Eich-Straße

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, the one tree on the street big enough to shape the view down it. It stands on Maria-Eich-Straße in Obermenzing, which is named for the pilgrimage oak at Planegg and not for this one.

trees.name: The Yew of Laimer Kirchweg
trees.story:
Nobody can tell you how old a yew is, and that is a property of the species rather than a gap in the paperwork. Yews grow slowly, then stop and start again for centuries, and the heartwood rots away from the middle while the tree stays perfectly healthy around it, so there is nothing left to count. Every part of it except the red flesh of the berry is poisonous, and it will resprout from a stump that would have finished any other tree here. Taxus baccata is the longest-lived thing that grows in Europe.

This one stands on Laimer Kirchweg, the old church path of a village that Munich has long since grown around, and the city's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it as a dominant tree that shapes the townscape. Yews and church paths belong together across Europe, usually with the tree older than the building at the end of the walk, though nothing on record connects this one to that habit.

Go in February. A yew keeps its dark, dense, almost black-green all winter, which is unremarkable in July and the only colour on the street in the dead of the year. The register lists no age and no girth, and if you know either, we would like to have it.
trees.transport: In Laim, on Laimer Kirchweg

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by dark, almost black-green foliage that holds its colour through winter, the only colour on the street in the dead of the year. It stands on Laimer Kirchweg.

trees.age_estimate: an enthusiast's estimate of around 250 years, unconfirmed

trees.story:
An American red oak thick enough to be one of Munich's largest hides behind a tennis club, a hundred metres north of the Fasanerie restaurant in Hartmannshofer Park, with no sign anywhere pointing to it. The city designated it a natural monument in 2021, citing simply that it is a very large red oak, rare anywhere inside Munich, after a resident first applied for its protection back in 2006. The paperwork took fifteen years to catch up with the tree.

Quercus rubra is native to eastern North America and was planted across German parks and forests from the 18th century on, valued for its fast growth and brilliant autumn colour rather than for any native pedigree. This one has done more with those decades than almost any other red oak in the city: 4.2 metres round at the base and about 30 metres tall, standing in a stretch of forest that has belonged to the Free State of Bavaria rather than the city since well before the park itself existed. A local tree enthusiast who pushed for its protection estimates it at around 250 years old, though nobody has confirmed that with a core sample or a planting record.

The park itself, the Hartmannshofer Wald, only became a public park in the 1960s. Before that it was simply forest, which may be exactly how this one tree got old enough to matter.

Age (~250 years) is explicitly a named local enthusiast's (Armin Peter) personal estimate, not a documented measurement or growth-rate derivation; stated as such and kept as a wide, flagged range rather than a precise figure.
