trees.story:
This lime was planted to celebrate a constitution, and it has outlived the kingdom that wrote it. On 20 May 1808 the citizens of Grünwald set it into their market square to mark King Max Joseph's new constitution for the Kingdom of Bavaria. A plaque on the trunk still records the gift.

That gives it something rare among old trees: a birthday. Most trees on this map carry an estimate or a range. This one has a date, which makes it about 218 years old in 2026, and the arithmetic is the whole argument.

It stands in the open where Grünwald's two main streets cross, a large-leaved lime with the town's traffic turning around it. Bavaria protects it twice over, as a natural monument and on the same footing as a listed building, an unusual honour for something that grows.

In the two centuries since, the constitution it was planted for was replaced and the Bavarian monarchy ended in 1918. The lime stayed where the citizens put it, on the square, with its plaque.

Nobody has published its girth or its height. If you pass with a tape measure, tell us what you find.

Grünwald lies about 12 km south of central Munich, so this is a suburban trip rather than a city stroll: tram 25 runs out from the centre, and the Marktplatz is a few minutes on foot from the stop.

trees.story:
The officials who protect this lime do not agree on which lime it is. The Landkreis München made it a natural monument by an ordinance of 22 February 1982, and the published list of the district's monuments calls it a Winterlinde, a small-leaved lime. The Bavarian state register, at the same spot by the chapel, names it a Sommerlinde, a large-leaved lime. The photographer who documented it in 2021 sided with the small-leaved reading, and so do we, but the dispute is real and still open.

What nobody disputes is where it stands. It grows on the street Auf der Eierwiese, directly beside the little chapel of St. John of Nepomuk, and its crown rises well over the chapel roof. Three separate coordinates, from the register, the list and geotagged photographs, land within a few metres of each other here.

You can settle the species yourself. A small-leaved lime has smaller, neater leaves and flowers in July; a large-leaved lime flowers a few weeks earlier, in June. Stand under it in early summer and the timing tells you. If you know it already, tell us which one it is.

No age, girth or height has been published for it either, so a measurement would be just as welcome.

The chapel is in Grünwald, about 12 km south of central Munich: a suburban trip on tram 25 from the centre, then on foot from the stop.

trees.story:
Most protected trees stand in parks or churchyards. This one stands beside a shopping arcade. The Landkreis München lists a single copper beech on Luitpoldweg in Grünwald as a natural monument, and it fills the open space at the western edge of the Schlosspassage.

That is the charm of it. You do not walk into a wood to find this tree. You step off tram 25 at its Grünwald terminus, roughly 100 metres away, and there it is above the forecourt, a tall dome of dark purple leaves among the shopfronts.

Copper beech is a colour form of the ordinary European beech, and the colour runs through the year: the leaves open purple in spring, darken through summer and turn copper before they fall.

The pin is close but not exact. The register gives a point for this one tree, and a 2021 photograph captioned at Luitpoldweg by the Schlosspassage shows it there, but no photograph carries its own position. In practice it matters little: look for the one large purple beech beside the arcade, with a red Japanese maple at its foot. The forecourt belongs to the shopping centre, so we cannot promise it is open at every hour, though the tree is plain to see from the square.

Nobody has published its age, girth or height. If you know any of the three, tell us.

Grünwald is about 12 km south of central Munich, a suburban trip by tram rather than a stroll from the centre.

This oak starts branching so low on its trunk that its crown has room to spread wide, and the photographer who documented it in 2021 left one piece of advice: see it from the west. That is where the spread shows best.

It stands at the side of Bergstraße in Oberhaching, where the road climbs east out of the Gleißental valley and a footpath called the Kirchweg branches off north behind the tree along the edge of the slope. The Landkreis München protects it as a natural monument. Part of the slope wood behind it is protected too, as a separate monument called the Elf Eichen, the Eleven Oaks, so this is plainly a corner where oaks were thought worth protecting.

The register says only Eiche, oak, without naming which one. If you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile oak by its acorn stalks, tell us.

The pin is close but not exact: the register and the district list agree to within two metres, but no photograph confirms the trunk independently. On the ground, look for the broad oak at the roadside exactly where the Kirchweg leaves Bergstraße, rather than the trees in the wood behind it. The address beside it, Bergstraße 7a, is a private house, so look from the road and leave the property alone.

No age, girth or height has been published.

trees.story:
Look up at the top of this ash and you will see a bare dead spire standing out of a green crown. When it was photographed in June 2023 the tree was in full leaf everywhere except that one leader at the summit. Whether storm or disease took it, nobody has said, and we will not guess. What the photograph shows is the rest of the tree alive and leafing.

It is a protected natural monument of the Landkreis München, a European ash at the corner of Wendelsteinstraße and Stefanusstraße in Gräfelfing, close to the bank of the Würm. An information board stands beside it, which is the surest sign you have the right tree. Its trunk leans and forks.

The pin is honest about its limits. The district's list and the Bavarian state register place the tree about 40 metres apart, both at the same junction, so our pin sits between them. At the corner, look for the tall ash with the dead spire and the board beside it.

Nobody has published its age, girth or height. If you know any of them, or if you pass and see how the crown is doing now, tell us.

trees.story:
This lime has a birth certificate of sorts: an information board gives the year it was planted, 1907. That makes it about 119 years old, and for once that is a date rather than an estimate.

Twenty-six years after it went into the ground, the Nazi regime opened a concentration camp on the edge of this town, and the name Dachau took on the meaning it still carries. The lime grew on in the old town through all of it, and through the liberation in April 1945. Today it stands on the corner of Konrad-Adenauer-Straße and Pfarrstraße, on the square called Widerstandsplatz, Resistance Square.

The Landkreis Dachau made it a natural monument in a 1997 ordinance, which names it a silver lime, a species from south-eastern Europe rather than a native. Its leaves are dark above and felted white beneath, so the crown flickers pale when the wind turns them over. It is also the last lime of the year to flower, in July, after the native limes have finished, and the honey scent carries across the square.

Nobody has published its girth or its height. If you stand under it with a tape measure, tell us what you find.

Dachau lies about 16 km north-west of central Munich: roughly 25 minutes on the S2, then a ten-minute walk from the station.

best_time.label: July, when the last lime of the summer flowers and the square smells of honey

trees.story:
This lime was protected as an inn's courtyard tree, and the inn has moved on without it. The county list that made it a natural monument places it in the courtyard of the Unterbräu on Augsburger Straße. A successor inn now trades there, and it no longer runs that yard, so today the tree stands at a street corner rather than in a guest garden.

The same list puts its age at about 140 years. It does not say when that figure was set or how, so read it loosely, somewhere between 120 and 160 years. Even at the low end it was in the ground before the First World War, a few steps off the main street of Dachau's old town, and it has stood there through every chapter of the town's twentieth century since.

The register calls it simply Linde, a lime, without naming which one. If you can tell a small-leaved from a large-leaved lime by the leaf, tell us.

Look for it at the corner of Gottesackerstraße and Färbergasse. Two separate map points for the tree agree to within about 11 metres. We have not seen where the old courtyard's fence runs today, so treat the corner as your viewpoint.

No girth or height has been published. Dachau is about 16 km north-west of central Munich: roughly 25 minutes on the S2, then a kilometre on foot from the station.

trees.story:
When it was photographed in mid-September 2023, this copper beech already had the thin crown of a tree in November. The photographer said so plainly in his caption: the tree did not look healthy, and its leaves were sparse before autumn leaf fall had even begun. It was alive that summer, in leaf if not in full leaf. How it looks today is something a visitor can tell us better than any record can.

It stands in Dachau's Alter Stadtfriedhof, the old town cemetery, and the county list that protects it as a natural monument gives directions rather than coordinates: about 20 metres inside the Jocherstraße entrance, on the left. Those directions and two separate map points agree on the spot, so this is one tree you will not have to hunt for among the graves.

The same list puts its age at about 160 years. That figure arrives without a date or a method attached, so read it as a band, somewhere between 140 and 190 years. Either way, it has spent well over a century among the town's graves.

A copper beech is the purple-leaved form of the common beech. No girth or height has been published for this one.

This is a working cemetery, so stand quietly and keep to the paths. It is about a kilometre on foot from Dachau station, which the S2 reaches from central Munich in roughly 25 minutes.

trees.story:
By the county's own estimate this oak is about 220 years old, and it lives fifteen metres from a railway embankment north of Dachau. Taken at face value, that puts its first years around 1806, when Bavaria became a kingdom. The figure comes without a date or a method, though, so treat it as a band, somewhere between 180 and 260 years.

It stands on the Leitenweg, a track north of the Leitenberg between Dachau and the village of Prittlbach. The list gives directions rather than coordinates: the north-east corner of a plot at the northern approach to the Leitenberg, about 15 metres from the embankment. Two map points for it sit about 43 metres apart, so our pin is a midpoint. Use the embankment as your guide.

We do not know whether the plot itself is open land, so plan to see the oak from the Leitenweg. If you have been, tell us whether you could walk up to the trunk.

The register says only Eiche, oak, without naming the species. If you can read it from the acorn stalks, tell us that too, along with a girth if you carry a tape.

This is not a stroll from the station. Take the S2 to Dachau, roughly 25 minutes from central Munich, then go about 3 km north on foot or by bike.

trees.story:
This is not one tree but a walk of limes clipped into a green tunnel, and by the county's estimate the limes are about 290 years old. The Landkreis Dachau protects it as a single natural monument, a geschnittener Lindenlaubengang, a clipped lime arbour, in the Hofgarten of Schloss Dachau.

That makes it a different kind of old. A lime left alone grows into a tall, rounded crown. These have been cut back and trained into a covered walk you can stand inside. If the county's figure holds, the limes went into the ground around the 1730s, and today they are held to a shape rather than left to grow. The estimate comes without a date or a method, so treat it as a band of roughly 250 to 320 years.

The list calls the trees only Linde, lime, and does not say which kind. If you can tell from the leaves, tell us, and the same goes for a trunk measurement.

The pin marks the palace garden rather than a particular trunk, but a covered lime walk is not something you will miss once you are inside. The garden is public; check its opening hours before you go. Schloss Dachau stands on the hill above the old town, roughly 1.5 km from Dachau station with a climb at the end, and the S2 reaches Dachau from central Munich in about 25 minutes.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shape: limes clipped and trained into a covered arbour walk, not free-standing crowns. It stands in the Hofgarten of Schloss Dachau, on the hill above the old town.

trees.story:
This oak marks a meeting of waters: it stands where the Entenbach runs into the Hachinger Bach, on the stretch of country between Taufkirchen and Unterhaching. The Landkreis München made it a natural monument in March 2020, and its list describes it by that confluence rather than by a house number.

It is a pedunculate oak, the long-stalked acorn oak of Central Europe, and the photographs taken of it in April 2022 and again in July 2026 show the trunk right on the bank of the stream, bare in spring, under a full green crown in summer. That is the whole of the record. The designation gives no age, no girth and no height, and the ordinance that may explain why it was chosen is no longer online.

So this is one to measure for us. If you carry a tape, a girth at chest height would let us estimate its age, and we would like to know it.

Come along the stream, not the road. The Münchner Straße here has no pavement, while a public path follows the Hachinger Bach past the trunk as part of the signposted Hachinger Bach walking route. From Unterhaching station on the S3 it is roughly 1.5 to 2 km on foot.

trees.story:
A king's daughter is said to have lived inside this tree for 35 years. The village of Puch tells it of Blessed Edigna, by tradition a daughter of a French king, who made her home in the hollow trunk and a cell beside it. The plaque gives her years as 1074 to 1109, and a small shrine to her is built into the trunk to this day.

How old the lime really is, nobody can say. The heartwood is gone, so there are no rings to count and nothing to carbon-date. A representative of the Deutsches Baumarchiv put it at 500 to 700 years in 2008; other estimates run to 1,000 or 1,200. Both camps are guessing from a ruin.

It has been pictured since the seventeenth century, including on the Bavarian survey sheet of 1861. A storm in 1880 broke one of its two main limbs, and the rotten part of the trunk was cut away in 1947. The old crown is gone. What stands now is a remnant stem roughly ten metres round, hard to measure because the shrine has grown into it, carrying a dense young crown some 20 metres high.

Farmers once fed its leaves to their cattle as blessed fodder, and since 1959 the village has staged Edigna plays every ten years. Our newest photograph is from 2018; if you have seen it since, tell us how it looks. Allow 45 to 55 minutes from Munich via the S4 to Fürstenfeldbruck.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small Edigna shrine built into the base of its trunk, behind a low iron fence. It stands in the churchyard of St. Sebastian in the middle of Puch.

trees.story:
Seven trunks rise from one base here, and together they measure about ten and a half metres round. Bavaria's list of remarkable trees calls this lime in Sauerlach a textbook example of multi-stemmed growth, and the figure from 2015 is the girth of all seven taken together, not of one trunk. The village's own Wikipedia article gives the same 10.5 metres as a diameter, which no lime on earth could manage; read it as a circumference.

It was a beer garden tree first. A photograph from 1930 shows it in the beer garden of the Gasthof zur Post. The inn's garden has since given way to a supermarket, and the lime stayed where it was, in front of the shop on Tegernseer Landstraße, across from the Alte Post. It is protected as a natural monument by the Landkreis München.

Its age is put at 180 to 200 years, though both figures trace back to a single source, and nobody records when it was planted. By that reckoning it has stood in the village centre since the early nineteenth century, through every change of use around it.

It is a large-leaved lime, the species that flowers first among Central Europe's limes. The S3 runs from Marienplatz to Sauerlach in about 30 minutes, and the tree is a five-minute walk from the station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its seven trunks rising together from one base. It stands in front of the supermarket at Tegernseer Landstraße 1 in the centre of Sauerlach, opposite the Alte Post.

trees.story:
The Landkreis Ebersberg protects this tree under a name that is also a description: Esche frei im Landschaftsbild stehend, the ash standing free in the landscape. It is natural monument number 41, and it earns the name. It stands alone at the edge of open fields, with a farm track beside it and a wayside cross at its foot, so the whole crown, 21 metres tall, stands clear against the sky.

The list it comes from says it was planted around 1870, which would make it roughly 150 years old, a date that travels through a single chain of sources and should be held loosely. In 2020 its trunk measured 4.90 metres round, a big girth for an ash of that age. If the planting date holds, it went into the ground around the time of the Franco-Prussian War and has spent its whole life marking the edge of the hamlet of Ingelsberg.

That life is not guaranteed. Ash dieback, a fungus that has killed ash trees across Europe, is at work in Bavaria. Photographs from August and December 2024 show this one standing, in full leaf in summer. If you visit, tell us how the crown looks; a report from the field is worth more to us than any register.

Take the S4 or S6 to Zorneding, about 25 minutes from Munich, then walk roughly 2 to 3 km out to Ingelsberg along rural paths. The cross beneath it is your landmark.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big ash in open fields with a wayside cross at the foot of its trunk. It stands just outside the hamlet of Ingelsberg, near Zorneding.

trees.story:
German Wikipedia calls this one of the most bizarre tree shapes in the country, and it is hard to argue. The Hollow Lime of Obermarbach is less a trunk than a shell of split, gaping wood, standing beside a sunken lane next to the village church of St. Vitus.

Bavaria's list of notable trees gives it a girth of 10.2 metres. Hold that number loosely: on a trunk this hollow and this split, the tape may have gone round a ring of separate pieces rather than one solid column, and the list does not say when it was measured.

The same list puts its age at about 400 years. That is a round estimate rather than a count, so read it as anywhere from 300 to 500. Near the middle of that band, it was already standing when the Thirty Years' War reached Bavaria in the 1630s. The list calls it only a lime and does not say which kind; if you can tell from the leaves, tell us.

It is a protected natural monument. The most recent photographs we can find of it were taken in June 2019, so a word on how it looks today would be welcome.

Obermarbach lies about 33 km north of Munich, in the municipality of Petershausen: a regional train from Munich to Petershausen, then a few kilometres on by bus or bike. It is further out than most trees on this page, and it does not look like any of them.

Two large-leaved limes stand together at the chapel of St. Aegidius in Grafing, and the larger of them has a trunk 7.90 metres round. Its partner measures 5.45 metres. Both figures come from a measurement taken in 2015 and recorded in Bavaria's list of notable trees, which gives each tree an age of about 260 years.

That age is an estimate, and the list does not say how it was reached, so read it as somewhere between 200 and 320 years. Near the middle of that band, the pair went into the ground in the middle of the eighteenth century, while Bavaria was still ruled by its electors, and they have grown side by side at the same chapel ever since. Landkreis Ebersberg protects them together as natural monument 81: one listing for two trees, which is also how they are best seen, from one spot.

Which of the two is the bigger, the left or the right as you face the chapel, is not recorded in anything we have read. A trunk of nearly eight metres should settle it at a glance; if you go, tell us which side it stands on. The latest photographs we know of date from October 2020, so a word on how both look now would help too.

Grafing is about 33 km east of Munich. The S4 or a regional train runs to Grafing Bahnhof, and the chapel on Am Stadion is roughly a kilometre on foot from there.

trees.story:
The cross at the foot of this lime still carries a prayer for field and house, written when the ground around it was grain fields. The fields are gone. Today it is a street near Dachau Stadt station, and when this tree was photographed in September 2023 the parked cars stood almost up against its trunk.

That pairing is the reason to come. The Landkreis Dachau protects the lime as a natural monument, and the photograph shows the tree and the wayside cross together, which is also the easiest way to be sure you have found the right one. The cross has outlasted the farming its prayer was written for.

The county list puts the lime at about 100 years, without a date or a method, so read that as a rough band of 90 to 130 years. By that estimate it has stood here through most of Dachau's twentieth century. The list calls it only Linde, a lime, and does not say which kind. If you know, tell us, and a girth or height would be welcome too, since neither has been published.

The list places it on Etzenhausener Straße, about 20 metres south of the turning into Prälat-Pfanzelt-Straße, and two map points agree to within a few metres. Look for the cross first. Dachau is about 25 minutes from central Munich on the S2.
